structure.unitsRequired: Unit 1 (mandatory) plus two of Units 2, 3 and 4
structure.terminalRule: At least 40% of the assessment (by unit weighting) must be taken in the series in which the final grade is requested (Spec §4.1).
structure.resits: Each unit may be resat once before cash-in; the better result counts unless the unit is needed for the 40% terminal rule, in which case the more recent mark counts (Spec §4.1).
structure.availability: Summer series only (Unit 1 from 2018; Units 2–4 from 2019); not offered in November/March series.
structure.priorAttainment: Students should ideally have covered all of the content in the CCEA GCSE Mathematics specification at Higher Tier, including all of the content of units M4 and M8 (Spec §1.3).

units.title: Unit 1: Pure Mathematics
units.assessment: External written examination in the form of a single question-and-answer booklet that includes a formula sheet
units.intro: In this unit, students investigate algebra, trigonometry, differentiation, integration, logarithms, matrices and quadratic inequalities.

units.title: Unit 2: Mechanics
units.assessment: External written examination in the form of a single question-and-answer booklet that includes a formula sheet
units.intro: In this unit, students explore kinematics, vectors, forces, Newton's Laws of Motion and moments.

units.title: Unit 3: Statistics
units.assessment: External written examination in the form of a single question-and-answer booklet that includes a formula sheet
units.intro: In this unit, students investigate central tendency and dispersion, probability, the binomial and normal distributions and bivariate analysis.

statements.text: add, subtract, multiply and divide rational algebraic fractions with linear and quadratic numerators and/or denominators;
statements.teacherGuidance: For example, simplify (x² − 3x)/3 × 9/(x² − x − 6).

statements.text: manipulate algebraic expressions, including the expansion of three linear brackets;
statements.teacherGuidance: For example, expand (2x + 1)(x − 3)(1 − 3x). Algebraic manipulation and formation can be assessed in a variety of ways.

statements.text: complete the square where the coefficient of x² will always be 1;
statements.teacherGuidance: (i) Rewrite f(x) = x² + 5x + 1 in the form (x + a)² + b.

statements.text: apply completing the square to solving quadratic equations and identifying minimum turning points;
statements.teacherGuidance: (ii) Use the completed-square form to find the minimum of f(x) and the value of x for which it occurs. (iii) Solve x² = −5x − 1 by completing the square, giving the answer in surd form, i.e., x = a ± √b or x = a ± c√b.

statements.text: form and solve three equations in three unknowns;
statements.teacherGuidance: The equations will be linear. Equations will be given or students may be asked to form the equations and interpret the results. Students should show the full development of their answer. Sole use of a calculator will not gain any marks.

statements.text: solve quadratic inequalities, which are restricted to quadratic expressions that factorise;
statements.teacherGuidance: Graphical method of solution is recommended. Formation of inequality may be required from a given context.

statements.text: sketch the graphs of sin x, cos x and tan x, where the range of x is a subset of −360° ≤ x ≤ 360°; and
statements.teacherGuidance: Only graphs of sin x, cos x and tan x are required. Transformations of these graphs, e.g., sin 2x, cos(x − 30°) will not be asked.

statements.text: solve simple trigonometric equations that lead to a maximum of two solutions in a given range.
statements.teacherGuidance: Example of equation: Solve cos(½x − 30°) = −0.7 in the range −360° ≤ x ≤ 360°. A variety of ranges will be used. Sine rule and cosine rule will not be asked.

statements.text: differentiate expressions that are restricted to integer powers of x;
statements.teacherGuidance: First and second derivatives may be asked. Note – fractional indices are excluded, all powers will be positive or negative integers.

statements.text: apply differentiation to: gradients; finding equations of tangents and normals at points on a curve; simple optimisation problems; and elementary curve sketching of a quadratic or cubic function;
subItems: finding equations of tangents and normals at points on a curve;
elementary curve sketching of a quadratic or cubic function;
statements.teacherGuidance: Three-dimensional optimisation problems and problems involving pi will not be asked. Cubic functions for sketching could have x as a common factor or be the product of 3 linear factors. Examples: y = x³ + 2x² − 5x or y = (x − 1)(x + 2)(2x − 3).

statements.text: demonstrate knowledge that integration is the inverse process to differentiation;
statements.teacherGuidance: Students will be asked to integrate the area between a curve, x-axis, and two ordinates x = a and x = b.

statements.text: integrate expressions that are restricted to integer powers of x, (x ≠ −1);
statements.note: The specification (and the Teacher Guidance) literally print the condition as (x ≠ −1); in context it means the power n ≠ −1, i.e. 1/x is not integrated.
statements.teacherGuidance: Powers are positive or negative integers only (see Differentiation); the integral of x⁻¹ is not required.

statements.text: form and evaluate definite integrals;
statements.teacherGuidance: Definite integrals are between two ordinates x = a and x = b.

statements.text: apply integration to finding the area under a curve;
statements.teacherGuidance: Students will be asked to integrate the area between a curve, x-axis, and two ordinates x = a and x = b. Excluding combinations of positive and negative areas.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of logarithms as a natural evolution from indices;
statements.teacherGuidance: Understand that 8 = 2³ ⇔ log₂ 8 = 3. Excluding change of base rule.

statements.text: solve problems using: the laws of logarithms; and log/log graphs in context;
statements.teacherGuidance: Excluding change of base rule. Students will be required to draw log/log graphs from a table of data. The resulting graph will be a straight line.

statements.text: solve indicial equations using logarithms;
statements.teacherGuidance: Example of indicial equation: Solve 3^(2x − 1) = 5^(1 + x). The powers in indicial equations will either be a constant or a linear expression in x.

statements.text: add, subtract and multiply matrices;
statements.teacherGuidance: Non square matrices may be used for addition or subtraction. Example: [2 3 4] + [5 −2 −7]. For multiplication, matrix dimensions will not exceed 3 rows or 3 columns, but 3 × 3 matrices will not be included.

statements.text: find the inverse of 2 × 2 matrices;
statements.teacherGuidance: Inverse of 2 × 2 matrices only (3 × 3 matrices are not included).

statements.text: solve matrix equations; and
statements.teacherGuidance: Matrix equations could be of the form: A ± X = B or AX = B or a combination of these. Equations of the form XA = B are excluded.

statements.text: use matrices to solve 2 × 2 simultaneous equations.
statements.teacherGuidance: Write the pair of linear equations as AX = B and solve with X = A⁻¹B (equations of the form XA = B are excluded).

statements.text: draw, interpret and use displacement/time graphs and velocity/time graphs;
statements.teacherGuidance: Including graphs showing two journeys, for example one vehicle meeting/overtaking another. Displacement/time graphs may include negative displacements while velocity/time graphs will only have positive velocity. Average speed and average velocity can be asked.

statements.text: use constant acceleration formulae;
statements.teacherGuidance: Including vertical and horizontal motion.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of the definition of vector and scalar quantities;
statements.teacherGuidance: A general definition (magnitude and direction vs magnitude only) with examples is expected; examiners accept 'quantity' for 'magnitude'.

statements.text: calculate the magnitude and direction of a vector;
statements.teacherGuidance: Including angle between xi + yj and either i or j.

statements.text: use i and j vectors in calculations;
statements.teacherGuidance: Including angle between xi + yj and either i or j.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding that force is a vector;
statements.teacherGuidance: Resolving problems and equilibrium problems involve a maximum of four separate forces.

statements.text: identify all forces acting on a body;
statements.teacherGuidance: Resolving problems and equilibrium problems involve a maximum of four separate forces.

statements.text: resolve forces into components;
statements.teacherGuidance: Resolving problems and equilibrium problems involve a maximum of four separate forces.

statements.text: find the resultant of a set of forces;
statements.teacherGuidance: Resolving problems and equilibrium problems involve a maximum of four separate forces.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of and apply the concept of equilibrium;
statements.teacherGuidance: Resolving problems and equilibrium problems involve a maximum of four separate forces.

statements.text: apply F = ma to the following scenarios: a body in horizontal or vertical motion; a body on an inclined plane; and two connected bodies in rectilinear motion; (F = μR will not be tested – if included, friction will be given as a value or as a value per unit mass, where appropriate.)
subItems: a body in horizontal or vertical motion;
a body on an inclined plane; and
two connected bodies in rectilinear motion;
statements.teacherGuidance: Straight line motion only. Including motion of a body on an inclined plane. Any externally applied forces acting on a body on an inclined plane will act parallel to that plane. Questions may involve calculating the magnitude of the resultant force exerted by a string on a pulley. With connected particles, either: both bodies move horizontally, or both bodies move vertically, or one body moves horizontally and the other moves vertically.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of the Principle of Moments and equilibrium of a rigid body (restricted to a horizontal uniform rod supported by one or two pivots).
statements.teacherGuidance: Problems will involve uniform rods only, no hinge or ladder questions.

statements.text: calculate the mean and standard deviation from data or estimates of these from grouped data;
statements.teacherGuidance: Calculation of median or interquartile range will not be asked.

statements.text: calculate the mean and standard deviation for combined sets of data;
statements.teacherGuidance: For example, a test given to a class of 6 boys and 4 girls resulted in an overall mean of 16.8. If the 6 boys achieved a mean mark of 16.0, find the mean mark achieved by the 4 girls.

statements.text: demonstrate knowledge of the effect on the mean and standard deviation of a linear transformation on a set of data;
statements.teacherGuidance: Know that if a data set is transformed such that Y = aX + b then ȳ = a x̄ + b and σ_Y = a σ_X. For example, given the mean and standard deviation for a data set, calculate the new mean and standard deviation if there is a change to the original data set, i.e., items removed or added.

statements.text: calculate combined probabilities using the addition rule, to include events that may not be mutually exclusive;
statements.teacherGuidance: Understand and use P(A ∪ B), P(A ∩ B) and P(A | B).

statements.text: calculate and interpret conditional probabilities using expected frequencies, two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams;
statements.teacherGuidance: Understand and use P(A ∪ B), P(A ∩ B) and P(A | B). Conditional probabilities can also be tested through the binomial and/or normal distributions.

statements.text: use the most appropriate method to solve complex problems, including the construction and use of Venn diagrams and tree diagrams;
statements.teacherGuidance: Conditional probabilities can also be tested through the binomial and/or normal distributions.

statements.text: use Pascal's triangle to expand (p + q)ⁿ where n ≤ 8;
statements.teacherGuidance: Example: A coin is tossed 7 times. The probability of obtaining a head on any one toss is 0.4. What is the probability that: i) a total of 1 or 2 heads is obtained [Prob (one head) + Prob (two heads)]; ii) at least 2 heads are obtained? [1 − Prob (no heads) − Prob (one head)].

statements.text: understand and use the binomial expansion to calculate probabilities in real-life contexts;
statements.teacherGuidance: The full derivation of binomial probabilities is required (coefficients from Pascal's triangle, powers of p and q shown).

statements.text: recognise that the distribution of many real-world variables takes the shape of a bell curve; and
statements.teacherGuidance: Students are encouraged to use a good diagram in the development of their answer.

statements.text: calculate a single probability from the normal distribution using tables and z = (x − μ)/σ where the mean and standard deviation are given.
statements.teacherGuidance: Probability will be of the form P(z > 1), P(z < −0.5) but not P(1 < z < 2). Students will only be required to find a probability from a z-value, not a z-value from a probability. Students are encouraged to use a good diagram in the development of their answer.

statements.text: calculate and interpret Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient;
statements.teacherGuidance: When interpreting Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient, r, know that −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 and that, for this specification, values −0.4 ≤ r ≤ 0.4 will be taken as weak or no correlation.

statements.text: draw the line of best fit by eye passing through (x̄, ȳ); and
statements.teacherGuidance: The plotting of original data will be given. Where possible, the line of best fit must always go through both means.

statements.text: calculate and use the equation of the line of best fit.
statements.teacherGuidance: Where possible, the line of best fit must always go through both means; use (x̄, ȳ) and a second point on the line to find the gradient.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of and use the addition and multiplication principles to count events in series and parallel respectively;
statements.teacherGuidance: Calculators may be used to calculate nCr and nPr.

statements.text: calculate the number of ways of arranging r objects from n objects;
statements.teacherGuidance: Calculators may be used to calculate nCr and nPr.

statements.text: calculate the number of ways of choosing r objects from n objects;
statements.teacherGuidance: Calculators may be used to calculate nCr and nPr.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of the concept of Boolean variables, including forming compound expressions using logical operators AND, OR and NOT;
statements.teacherGuidance: No further elaboration given in the Teacher Guidance.

statements.text: use truth tables to prove the equivalence of propositional statements (involving no more than three variables);
statements.teacherGuidance: No further elaboration given in the Teacher Guidance.

statements.text: model real-life scenarios as linear programming problems;
statements.teacherGuidance: No further elaboration given in the Teacher Guidance.

statements.text: use graphical methods to maximise or minimise an expression involving up to five inequalities in one or two variables (solutions may be real numbers or restricted to integers);
statements.teacherGuidance: No further elaboration given in the Teacher Guidance.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of why we smooth data;
statements.teacherGuidance: The correct trend line will always be a straight line.

statements.text: calculate appropriate moving averages (using three, four or five points); and
statements.teacherGuidance: The correct trend line will always be a straight line.

statements.text: draw a trend line and use it to make predictions (the plotting of original data will be given).
statements.teacherGuidance: The correct trend line will always be a straight line.

statements.text: demonstrate understanding of how an activity network represents a project (using activities on an arc);
statements.teacherGuidance: Scheduling will be able to be performed by inspection.

statements.text: construct an activity network from a precedence table;
statements.teacherGuidance: Activity-on-arc networks.

statements.text: identify the critical path by finding the earliest and latest event times;
statements.teacherGuidance: Forward pass for earliest event times, backward pass for latest event times.

statements.text: calculate float times; and
statements.teacherGuidance: Float = latest finish − earliest start − duration; critical activities have zero float.

statements.text: perform basic scheduling using Gantt charts.
statements.teacherGuidance: Scheduling will be able to be performed by inspection.

topics.title: Simplifying algebraic fractions

examinerEvidence.note: Q8: first step must be to factorise all quadratics; many failed and 'tied themselves up in knots with cubic numerators and denominators'; incorrect cancelling evident.
Q8(a): most factorised and cancelled but a high number did not simplify fully, missing the factor of 2.
Q9: several failed to fully simplify, leaving 3x(x − 2)/x as the final answer.

mustMemorise: Factorise every numerator and denominator before cancelling
Only common factors (not terms) cancel
Difference of two squares a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions

examinerEvidence.note: Q9(b): majority knew to invert the right-hand fraction and factorise, but 4x² − 1 was commonly left unfactorised; weaker candidates expanded everything.
Q9: most replaced division by multiplication by the inverted fraction; cancellation of terms then caused problems.
Q8(a): incorrect cancelling of terms and incomplete simplification.

mustMemorise: To divide, invert the second fraction and multiply
Factorise first, then cancel across the product

topics.title: Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions

examinerEvidence.note: Q8: weak algebra most evident here; incorrect cancelling when adding the two fractions; more practice required.
Q12: errors gathering terms in the numerator; those who divided by 3 before factorising got x(x + 2) wrongly; 'candidates generally need more practice with algebraic expressions'.
Q9(a): many lost the final mark by failing to subtract all terms of the quadratic from the cubic; some divided the correct answer by 2.
Q9: took a common denominator but failed to recognise the numerator as a difference of two squares.
Q8(b): did not use (x + 3)(x − 3) as the lowest common denominator for x² − 9, producing cubics they could not handle; cancelling before adding.

Q7: very few full marks; x(x + 3) − (x − 3)(x + 4) mis-expanded to x² + 3x − x² + x + 12 (sign not applied across the bracket); dropped brackets; premature cancelling; stopping short of the final value 2.

mustMemorise: Lowest common denominator uses each factor once (factorise x² − 9 first)
Put brackets round a subtracted numerator and change every sign
Simplify the final numerator and cancel

topics.title: Expanding three linear brackets

examinerEvidence.note: Q12(i): well done, most expanded the brackets successfully.
Q9(a): most correctly expanded the cubic and quadratic expressions.
Q12(iii): answered well even by weaker candidates, though a few made mistakes by not using brackets around terms.

mustMemorise: Expand two brackets first, then multiply the quadratic by the third bracket term by term
Collect like terms in descending powers

topics.title: Completing the square (coefficient of x² = 1)

examinerEvidence.note: Q2(i): straightforward but more candidates than expected were unfamiliar with completing the square.
Q2: very well answered; notable errors were adding 49 instead of subtracting and writing 7 instead of −7.
Q3(i): most completed the square; common error writing (x + 3/2)² with the wrong constant term through poor arithmetic.

mustMemorise: x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c

topics.title: Minimum point from the completed square

examinerEvidence.note: Q2(ii): some could not interpret the minimum value and the corresponding x; some differentiated instead.

Q4(ii): many lost both marks by differentiating instead of using the completed square as required; others substituted x = 4 back into the original equation rather than reading y from the completed square.
Q3(ii): 'hence' required the Part (i) result; those who used calculus scored zero even when mathematically correct.

mustMemorise: (x + a)² + b has minimum value b at x = −a
When the question says 'hence', the completed-square method is compulsory

topics.title: Solving quadratics by completing the square (surd answers)

examinerEvidence.note: Q8: completing the square was very well done as the equation to solve was given.
Q6(ii): generally well done with the method clearly shown; a small number used the quadratic formula instead of the required method.

mustMemorise: Answer form x = a ± √b or x = a ± c√b
Simplify surds, e.g. √20 = 2√5
Do not switch to the quadratic formula when completing the square is specified
onFormulaSheet: Quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a (Unit 1 formula sheet)

topics.title: Solving three linear equations in three unknowns

examinerEvidence.note: Q7: nearly all knew to eliminate variables and back-substitute; arithmetic errors the main cause of wrong answers.
Q11(iv): a lot of candidates, even weaker ones, obtained full marks.
Q11(iv): solved with few errors, but many forgot to multiply back by 1000; values 'worked out on a calculator with no method' gained no marks.
Q12(iii): arithmetic errors; calculator-only answers gained no marks; fractional answers lost the final mark.

mustMemorise: Eliminate one unknown from two pairs of equations, solve the resulting 2 × 2 system, then back-substitute
Show every elimination step – sole use of a calculator gains no marks

topics.title: Forming three equations from a context and interpreting solutions

examinerEvidence.note: Q10: forming the second equation was poorly done (x + y − z = 55 common); 'show that' steps set out poorly; candidates did not check that very large or negative values were meaningless.
Q11(ii)–(iii): many could not translate '£8 dearer' or '50% greater' into algebra; parts often omitted.
Q11(i)–(iii): often poorly answered; percentage signs confused candidates; working backwards from the given equations gains no marks.
Q11(i)–(iii): multiplying rather than dividing to reach the given equation; thousands on the right-hand side caused problems.
Q12(iv): currency conversion with a 40% decrease was 'the most poorly answered part of the entire paper'.

mustMemorise: Define the three unknowns with units before writing equations
'a is 50% greater than b' → a = 1.5b; 'a is £8 dearer than b' → a = b + 8
Scale answers back (e.g. × 1000) and sanity-check them in context

topics.title: Solving quadratic inequalities

examinerEvidence.note: Q4: too many failed to bring the 5 across to make one side zero (loss of all marks); inequality sign mishandled after finding critical values −3 and 1.5.
Q6: most solved the quadratic; not all drew a sketch, which would help identify the correct region.
Q7: negative x² coefficient caused confusion; wrong graph drawn; shading the solution region on the sketch recommended.
Q5: most derived and solved the inequality but lost the final mark by not excluding negative x in the context.
Q3: inequality sign lost and treated as an equation; no sketch led to the wrong region.
Q4: more successful than previous years; errors were failing to interpret the critical values as a region (e.g. −5/2 < x < 6 vs x > 6 and x < −5/2).

mustMemorise: Rearrange to (quadratic) > 0 or < 0 with zero on one side
Factorise to find critical values, sketch, then read the region
'Between the roots' for < 0 when the x² coefficient is positive; two outer regions for > 0

topics.title: Sketching the graphs of sin x, cos x and tan x

examinerEvidence.note: Q3(a): sine graph drawn with sides too straight; many gained the mark for points only.
Q4(a): cosine curve too straight between max and min; axes should show −90°, 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360° and ±1.
Q4(a): quite a few omitted scales on the axes and some inverted the sine graph.
Q3(a): no indication of turning points at ±180°; sketch looked like a straight line heading below −1; no y-scale.
Q2(a): tan graph 'particularly problematic' – asymptotes omitted or placed at 180°, curves touching/crossing asymptotes, sine-like shapes.

mustMemorise: Shapes, periods (360° for sin/cos, 180° for tan) and key values
tan has vertical asymptotes at ±90°, ±270° and passes through 0°, ±180°, ±360°
Label both axes with a scale

topics.title: Solving simple trigonometric equations in a given range

examinerEvidence.note: Q3(b): common wrong answers 60° and 300°; difficulties using CAST with a negative value; poor rearranging to make x the subject.
Q4(b): a few used 0.184 instead of −0.184; follow-through produced a second answer outside the range.
Q4(b)(i): majority scored only one mark – found 53.13° but could not select the angles in the range; the sketch from part (a) gives a visual check.
Q3(b): some used cos⁻¹(2/3) with the wrong sign; dividing by 2 instead of multiplying when isolating x.
Q4: well answered; a common error was to multiply by 2 then add 20 in the wrong order.
Q2(b)(i): tan⁻¹(6) = 80.54° given alone without the second solution; adding/subtracting from 90° gave answers outside the range.

mustMemorise: Find the base angle, then use the graph/CAST to find the second solution (sin: 180° − α; cos: −α or 360° − α; tan: α + 180°)
Solve for the bracket first, then undo the transformation in reverse order
Reject solutions outside the given range

topics.title: Differentiating integer powers of x (first and second derivatives)

examinerEvidence.note: Q1: well done; fraction and negative power handled well by the majority.
Q3(i): few problems, though answers such as 8/6 x should be simplified; Q11: some could not differentiate −3x⁻¹ and read the gradient as −3 from y = mx + c.
Q1(i): moving the index term to the top line and then differentiating it caused a lot of problems.
Q8(i): errors with the power rule (x⁻² instead of x⁻⁴) and constants (+12 instead of −12).

mustMemorise: Rewrite a/xⁿ as ax⁻ⁿ before differentiating
d/dx(axⁿ) = naxⁿ⁻¹; derivative of a constant is 0
Second derivative d²y/dx² = differentiate again
onFormulaSheet: If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹ (Unit 1 formula sheet)

topics.title: Gradient of a curve at a point

examinerEvidence.note: Q8(ii): surprisingly few could take the first step of writing the gradient of the tangent as −8.
Q13(i): many set dy/dx = 0 'out of habit' instead of dy/dx = 5 to find where the gradient is 5; Q8(ii): substituting y into an equation involving dy/dx was poorly answered.

mustMemorise: Gradient at x = a is dy/dx evaluated at x = a
To find where the gradient has a given value, set dy/dx equal to that value (not zero)
onFormulaSheet: If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹ (Unit 1 formula sheet)

topics.title: Equations of tangents and normals

examinerEvidence.note: Q11: good discriminator; 'candidates need more practice in determining the equation of a normal'; credit given for knowing the normal gradient is the negative reciprocal.
Q8(ii): only the stronger candidates scored well.
Q10: advance information said 'normal', so answers were noticeably better; slips in the gradient at x = −1 and in the constant.
Q9: only a minority full marks; many set the line equal to the curve instead of differentiating; used the given gradient of 3 wrongly, so the normal gradient was wrong.
Q13(ii): perpendicular gradient −1/5 usually found, but some stopped there or wrote a line equation instead of the required coordinates.

mustMemorise: Tangent gradient m = dy/dx at the point; normal gradient = −1/m
y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
A line with given gradient meets the curve where dy/dx equals that gradient
onFormulaSheet: If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹ (Unit 1 formula sheet)

topics.title: Stationary points and their nature

examinerEvidence.note: Q8(ii): arithmetic slips finding the y-value at x = −5/9; two maxima or two minima should have signalled an error.
Q10(i): some wrote down first and second derivatives but did not know what to do with them.
Q12(iv)–(v): differentiate, set to zero, second derivative for nature – many full marks with follow-through; Q14(ii): many did not use the second derivative to show the maximum at t = 3.
Q11(ii): a few lost marks for not writing the turning point as a coordinate.

mustMemorise: Set dy/dx = 0 and solve
d²y/dx² > 0 minimum, < 0 maximum
Give turning points as coordinates (x, y)

markingConventions.M: Method mark – awarded for a correct method (an appropriate equation, formula or process), even if the arithmetic that follows is wrong.
markingConventions.W: Working/accuracy mark – awarded for accurate working or a correct value that follows from the method.
markingConventions.MW: Combined method-and-working mark – awarded only when the method is correct and carried out accurately.
notes: Calculator-only answers with no method score nothing if wrong: 'if the solution is incorrect then they cannot gain any method marks as no method has been shown' (CER 2023); 'Sole use of a calculator will not gain any marks' (Teacher Guidance, simultaneous equations).
Follow-through marking applies after an error; positive marking – credit is given for what is correct.
Where an error trivialises a question, not more than half the marks are usually awarded; a misread that makes a question easier earns only a proportion of the marks.

Method-locked questions: when the question says 'hence', 'use matrices', 'by completing the square' or 'show that', an alternative method (even if mathematically correct) receives no marks; working backwards from a given answer in a 'show that' gains no marks.
Rounding: 'Where rounding is necessary give answers correct to 2 decimal places unless stated otherwise'; log/log tables to 3 decimal places; do not truncate or round intermediate values.
Bold text in a question is a hint to read carefully; final answers go on the answer line; units and money notation where appropriate.
All working must be clearly shown; marks may be awarded for partially correct solutions (front-cover instructions).
Force diagrams: every force needs an arrow and a label; missing or extra forces are penalised (CER 2019–2025).
